claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically contains porosity and grain-boundary imperfections.
Porosity and grain-boundary imperfections promote ZrB2 component failure under corrosive conditions.
ZrB2 specimens have previously been fabricated using high-energy ball milling and SPS.
Optimized SPS can consolidate single-phase ZrB2 at approximately 2000–2100 °C.
Optimized SPS pulse current, pressure, and reduced dwell time promote accelerated densification of ZrB2.
Pulsed electric current and applied pressure accelerate mass transport and densification kinetics.
Lower SPS temperatures limit high-temperature grain growth and defect formation in ZrB2.
Optimized SPS produces a refined, highly dense ZrB2 microstructure with reduced pore and grain-boundary defect density.
The density of the cited SPS-fabricated ZrB2 benchmarking specimen was generally uniform at different locations.
A refined, dense ZrB2 microstructure is more resistant to corrosion in a liquid plating bath.
Chemical corrosion and mechanical stresses during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure cause holes to develop in ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit less initiation and propagation of corrosion-induced holes than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Reducing corrosion-induced hole formation will enhance the structural integrity of ZrB2 during long-duration plating-bath exposure.
SPS-processed ZrB2 prepared at 2000–2100 °C will achieve phase purity comparable to conventionally sintered ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 prepared at 2000–2100 °C will achieve mechanical strength comparable to or better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The hardness of the cited SPS-fabricated ZrB2 specimen was generally uniform at different specimen locations.
SPS is known to enable lower sintering temperatures and refined microstructures in similar material systems.
